This British Conservative served as Leader of the House of Commons from 2022 to 2024, ran for party leadership against Liz Truss, and later lost her Portsmouth North seat in 2024 — who is she?
In 1996, a gunman killed 35 people at a historic Tasmanian tourist site, leading to sweeping changes in Australia's gun laws — what is this tragedy called?
Port Arthur massacre: 1996 mass shooting in Tasmania, Australia.
Serving as Ecuador's president from 2007 to 2017, this democratic socialist economist has lived in Belgium since leaving office — who is he?
Rafael Correa: President of Ecuador from 2007 to 2017. Correa won the presidency in the 2006 general election on a platform criticizing the established political elites.
Designated Crown Prince during his father's 1967 coronation, this dissident has lived in exile in the US since the 1979 revolution that abolished the monarchy his family once ruled — who is he?
Reza Pahlavi: Former Crown Prince of Iran (born 1960)
Valedictorian of Plains High School in Georgia, this American first lady became a lifelong champion of mental health and women's rights — who was she?
Rosalynn Carter: First Lady of the United States from 1977 to 1981.
Nominated by President George W. Bush in 2005, this jurist became just the second Italian American justice on the Supreme Court, after Antonin Scalia — who is he?
Samuel Alito: US Supreme Court justice since 2006.
This Neo-Assyrian king destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and rebuilt Nineveh into a grand capital, but is most famous in the Hebrew Bible for his campaign in the Levant. Who was he?
Sennacherib: King of Assyria. Shortly after Sennacherib inherited the throne in 705 BC, Marduk-apla-iddina retook Babylon and allied with the Elamites.

During the Congo Crisis in 1961, a company of Irish UN peacekeepers was surrounded for five days by Katangese forces near a mining town before surrendering for lack of ammunition and water — which battle is this?
Siege of Jadotville: 1961 battle between Irish UN troops and Katanga during Congo Crisis.

Elected king of Poland in 1764 with the backing of Catherine the Great — with whom he'd become intimately involved at the Russian court — he became the last monarch of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; who was he?
Stanisław August Poniatowski: Ruler of Poland–Lithuania from 1764 to 1795.
Led by a man who declared himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, this 1850s Chinese theocratic state waged a 14-year war against the Qing dynasty — what was it?
Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: Theocratic monarchy in China (1851–1864)
A Whig historian famed for his prose, he both wrote a seminal "History of England" and played a major role in shaping India's education policy — who was he?
Thomas Babington Macaulay: British historian and politician (1800–1859)
What is this — “1938 spree killing in Japan”?
Tsuyama massacre: 1938 spree killing in Japan. It is the deadliest shooting by a lone gunman in Japanese history.
This French Romantic giant gave the world both 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame' and a sprawling 1862 novel that became a beloved musical — who was he?
Victor Hugo: French writer and politician (1802–1885)
Nicknamed the "Land Cruiser War," this conflict erupted in Sudan in 2003 and led to President Omar al-Bashir being indicted for genocide by the International Criminal Court. What was it?
War in Darfur: Genocidal conflict in Western Sudan.
Also known as the Prince of Orange, he led the Dutch revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule that ignited the Eighty Years' War and eventually won the United Provinces their independence — who is he?
William the Silent: Dutch revolt leader (1533–1584)

Born to a family of strawberry farmers in Akita Prefecture, this politician rose to become Japan's Prime Minister from 2020 to 2021 after years as Chief Cabinet Secretary under Shinzo Abe — who is he?

Yoshihide Suga: Prime Minister of Japan from 2020 to 2021. Yoshihide Suga (菅 義偉, Suga Yoshihide; born 6 December 1948) is a Japanese former politician who served as Prime Minister of Japan from 2020 to 2021.
Who among these was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
William Osler (born 1849) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the oldest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these is a physicist?
Max von Laue is a physicist.
Which of these is a chemist?
Alfred Nobel is a chemist. Alfred Bernhard Nobel ( noh-BEL; Swedish: [ˈǎlːfrɛd nʊˈbɛlː]; 21 October 1833 – 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
What is the atomic number of Einsteinium?
Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Es and atomic number 99 and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element.
In what year was Hamish Harding born?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year was Vikram Sarabhai born?
Vikram Sarabhai: Often regarded as the "Father of Indian space program", Sarabhai was honored with Padma Bhushan in 1966 and the Padma Vibhushan (posthumously) in 1972.
In what year was Johann Wolfgang von Goethe born?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (28 August 1749 – 22 March 1832) was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
In what year did Aryabhata die?
Aryabhata: The claim that Nalanda used to be located in Kusamapura/Pataliputra also cannot be proven.
In what year did Ivan Pavlov die?
Ivan Pavlov: Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
In what year was Iodine discovered?
Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
In what year was Nickel discovered?
Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.
Magnesium sulfate: Pfizer. It is a white crystalline solid, soluble in water.
In which country is Fish and chips?
Fish and chips: United Kingdom. Fish and chips is a hot dish consisting of battered and fried fish, served with chips.
Who is credited with discovering Norma?

Norma (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for normal, referring to a right angle, and is variously considered to represent a rule, a carpenter's square, a set square or a level.
Who is credited with discovering Aspartame?
Aspartame: James M. Schlatter. Aspartame is an artificial, non-saccharide sweetener commonly used as a sugar substitute in foods and beverages.
Who is credited with discovering Histamine?
Histamine: Henry Hallett Dale. Histamine or histamin is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.
About 5 million tonnes of acetic acid are produced annually largely to make this compound, most commonly in polymer form — what is it?
Acetate is a salt formed by the combination of acetic acid with a base (e.g. sodium hydroxide), an ester of acetic acid, or the anion CH3COO- found in solution.
First approved in the United States in 1966, this xanthine oxidase inhibitor treats high uric acid levels linked to gout, kidney stones, and chemotherapy — what medication is it?
Allopurinol is a medication used to decrease high blood uric acid levels.
Nicknamed the 'nail mosquito,' this genus — first classified in 1818 — is the sole mosquito genus known to carry human malaria — which genus is it?
Anopheles is a genus of mosquito first described by the German entomologist J. W. Meigen in 1818.
This medical condition, most often caused in the developed world by liver cirrhosis, is the abnormal buildup of fluid within the abdominal cavity — what is it called?
Ascites is the abnormal build-up of fluid in the abdomen.

Ranking among the largest wild cats, this population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies has roamed the Indian subcontinent since the Late Pleistocene and is found from India to southwestern China — name it?
Bengal tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies. It is distributed from India, southern Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan to Southwestern China.
This rigid, mineralized organ of the vertebrate skeleton produces both red and white blood cells and helps regulate the body's acid-base balance — what is it?
Bone is a rigid organ that constitutes part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals.
This soft, silvery-white metal shares group 12 of the periodic table with zinc and mercury, resembling zinc in its chemistry and mercury in its low melting point — what element, symbol Cd, is it?
Cadmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cd and atomic number 48.
This neuropsychiatric syndrome, often linked to mood or psychotic disorders, can leave a person nearly motionless for days or cause repetitive, purposeless movements. What is it?
Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome most commonly seen in people with underlying mood disorders such as major depressive disorder, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.
Native to East Asia and blooming late in the season, these autumn flowers of the daisy family are associated in the Northern Hemisphere with the month of November. What flower is it?
Chrysanthemum (kriss-), sometimes abbreviated to mums or chrysanths, are perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the family Asteraceae that bloom in the autumn.
This highly poisonous member of the carrot family can grow to nearly 8 feet tall, with hollow, maroon-spotted stems and a famously unpleasant odor — what plant is it?
Conium maculatum (British English) or poison hemlock (in North America), is a highly poisonous flowering plant and a nitrophile weed species in the carrot family Apiaceae.
This Zambian-born economist turned four of her five books into New York Times bestsellers, including a provocative argument that foreign aid actually holds Africa back — who is she?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo (born 2 February 1969) is a Zambian-born economist and author, known for her analysis of macroeconomics and global affairs.
This Canadian optical physicist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing chirped pulse amplification, a breakthrough in pulsed lasers. Who is she?
Donna Strickland (born May 27, 1959) is a Canadian optical physicist and pioneer in the field of pulsed lasers.

This German chess champion — also a mathematician and philosopher — held the world title for 27 years, the longest reign ever, and was famed for a 'psychological' approach said to unsettle opponents. Who was he?
Emanuel Lasker (German; December 24, 1868 - January 11, 1941) was a German chess player, mathematician, and philosopher.
Distinct from secretion, this bodily process includes exhaling carbon dioxide, sweating, and passing urine through the bladder and urethra — what's it called?
Excretion is elimination of metabolic waste, which is an essential process in all organisms.
This American physician-scientist discovered genes tied to several diseases, led the Human Genome Project, and went on to direct the NIH under three presidents — who is he?
Francis Collins (born April 14, 1950) is an American physician-scientist who discovered the genes associated with a number of diseases and led the Human Genome Project.
This flowering plant genus, whose name derives from the Latin word for a small sword, belongs to the iris family and is centered on the Cape Floristic Region of South Africa — which genus?
Gladiolus (from Latin, the diminutive of gladius, a sword) is a genus of perennial cormous flowering plants in the iris family (Iridaceae).
This flatfish's English name blends words for 'holy' and 'flat fish,' a nod to its place on the Catholic holy-day menu. Which bottom-dwelling fish?
Halibut is the common name for three species of flatfish in the family of right-eye flounders.
Nesting monogamously in tree cavities across Africa, Asia, and Melanesia, these birds are unique for having their first two neck vertebrae fused solid — which birds?
Hornbill are birds found in tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia and Melanesia of the family Bucerotidae.
Supplied by the lumbar spinal nerves and part of the femoral nerve, this fused pair of abdominal and thigh muscles is the body's strongest hip flexor — what is it called?
Iliopsoas (from Latin ile 'groin' and Ancient Greek (ps) 'muscles of the loins') refers to the joined psoas major and the iliacus muscles.
Most of the flowers used by the global perfume industry for this fragrant genus of shrubs and vines are grown in a single Egyptian village. What plant is it?
Jasmine (botanical name: Jasminum) is a genus of shrubs and vines in the olive family of Oleaceae.

This childhood illness of unknown cause mainly affects kids under five, causing a prolonged fever lasting more than five days that doesn't respond to typical fever-reducing medicine, plus inflamed blood vessels throughout the body — name the syndrome?
Kawasaki disease (also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) is a syndrome of unknown cause that results in a fever and mainly affects children under 5 years of age.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Born in Winnipeg and trained at King's College London, this physicist and chemist joined the Manhattan Project in 1942 to conduct experiments with uranium — who is he?
Louis Slotin (1 December 1910 - 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
This Italian economist served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022 after previously heading the European Central Bank for eight years and the Bank of Italy before that — who is he?

Mario Draghi (born 3 September 1947) is an Italian politician, economist, academic, banker, statesman, and civil servant, who served as the prime minister of Italy from 13 February 2021 to 22 October 2022.
Despite little formal education, this self-made English scientist established the concept of the electromagnetic field and uncovered the principles behind electromagnetic induction — who is he?
Michael Faraday (22 September 1791 - 25 August 1867) was an English chemist and physicist who contributed vastly to the study of electrochemistry and electromagnetism.

Though its 83 species can grow as tall as trees, this genus is technically herbaceous, its 'trunk' just tightly wrapped leaf stalks, and it gives us edible bananas, plantains, and fiber for cloth — what genus is it?
Musa (plant) is one of three genera in the family Musaceae.

First described in 1766 by naturalist Peter Simon Pallas, this sole living member of its genus sports a white throat patch and, in males only, a pair of short horns — what is this large Asian antelope called?
Nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus) (literally meaning "blue cow") is the largest antelope in Asia.
Also covering the modification of facial growth known as dentofacial orthopedics, this branch of dentistry corrects mal-positioned teeth and bite patterns. What field is it?

Orthodontics (also referred to as orthodontia) is a dentistry specialty that addresses the diagnosis, prevention, management, and correction of mal-positioned teeth and jaws, as well as misaligned bite patterns.

The males of this Phasianidae bird are famed for piercing calls and extravagant plumage; its Asiatic species include blue, green, and a third found only in the Congo Basin — what is this bird, collectively?

Peafowl is a common name for two bird species of the genus Pavo and one species of the closely related genus Afropavo within the tribe Pavonini of the family Phasianidae (the pheasants and their allies).

A pnictogen with only one stable isotope and atomic number 15, this element hides in Earth's crust mostly as phosphate rock and readily builds a vast family of organic and inorganic compounds. Which element is it?
Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.
Known as little hogweed or pursley, every part of this succulent plant can be eaten raw or cooked — what plant is it?
Portulaca oleracea (common purslane, also known as little hogweed, or pursley) is a succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae.
This kidney inflammation, most often caused by E. coli infection, typically causes fever and tenderness along the side of the body — what is it?
Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney, typically due to a bacterial infection.
Home to about 200 species — among them the plants we call currants and gooseberries — this genus is the sole member of its own plant family — which genus?
Ribes is a genus of approximately 200 known species of flowering plants, predominantly native to the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Arising from connective tissues like bone, cartilage, muscle, and fat, this rare cancer of mesenchymal cells makes up just 1% of adult diagnoses but 15% of childhood ones. What is it?
Sarcoma is a rare type of cancer that arises from cells of mesenchymal origin.

This medical state of insufficient blood flow to body tissues comes in four main types, from hypovolemic to cardiogenic, and can progress from weakness and rapid breathing to confusion or cardiac arrest. What is this condition called?
Shock (circulatory) is the state of insufficient blood flow to the tissues of the body as a result of problems with the circulatory system.

Some versions allow a 'tie' or 'draw' while others insist on a single winner; it can pit hundreds against each other or just one person against the clock — what do we call this organized physical activity?
Sport is a physical activity or game, often competitive and organized, that maintains or improves physical ability and skills.
Also called 'true comfrey,' this Boraginaceae perennial is native to damp European meadows and popular with bumblebees, despite carrying warnings about liver toxicity if eaten — which plant?
Symphytum officinale is a perennial flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae.

In 1933 he won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries about the role of chromosomes in heredity, studying fruit-fly genetics after the rediscovery of Mendelian inheritance in 1900—who was this pioneering biologist?
Thomas Hunt Morgan (September 25, 1866 - December 4, 1945) was an American evolutionary biologist, geneticist, and embryologist.
First isolated as a metal in 1783, this element is drawn from ores like scheelite and wolframite — the latter lending it an alternative name. Which metal is it?
Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from) and atomic number 74.

This forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth can result from food poisoning, pregnancy, motion sickness, or more serious causes like brain tumors, and is usually preceded by nausea — name this bodily reaction?
Vomiting (scientifically known as emesis, and otherwise known as puking, and throwing up) is the forceful expulsion of the contents of one's stomach through the mouth and sometimes the nose.
Twice Egypt's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, this archaeologist has dug across the Nile Delta, the Western Desert, and the Upper Nile Valley — who is he?
Zahi Hawass (born May 28, 1947) is an Egyptian archaeologist, Egyptologist, and former Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, a position he held twice.
Widespread across Europe and into East Asia, this venomous snake looms large in British folklore but rarely delivers a fatal bite — what reptile?
Adder: Species of venomous snake. Vipera berus, commonly known as the common European adder and the common European viper, is a species of venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
This Italian physicist built the first true electric battery in 1799 and discovered methane, disproving the idea that electricity could only come from living bodies — who is he?
Alessandro Volta: Italian chemist and physicist (1745–1827)
Formed naturally around volcanic vents and on burning coal dumps, this white crystalline salt is mildly acidic in solution and is used as both a fertilizer and food additive — which compound?
Ammonium chloride: Chemical compound. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.
Bridging biology and sociology, this scientific study of humanity has social, cultural, linguistic and biological branches, and treats archaeology as the study of the human past — what's the field?
Anthropology: Scientific study of humans, human behavior, and societies.
This Russian designer and outspoken blogger, known for provocative and often obscene commentary, founded a namesake design studio and is a descendant of the Tolstoy family — who is he?
Artemy Lebedev: Russian designer and businessman (born 1975)
Sold as Zithromax, this antibiotic tackles strep throat, pneumonia and traveler's diarrhea — but its tendency to cause QT prolongation keeps doctors watchful of the heart. Which drug is it?
Azithromycin: Antibiotic. It is administered by mouth, into a vein, or as topical treatment for the eye.
Commonly known as barberry, this genus of deciduous and evergreen shrubs grows worldwide except Australia, and one of its species is Oregon's official state flower — what genus is it?
Berberis: Genus of flowering plants representing the barberry family.

Native to North America and classified in the genus Vaccinium, this fruit comes in wild 'lowbush' and cultivated 'highbush' varieties, with Canada leading global production of the wild type — what fruit is it?
Blueberry: Perennial plant with blue berries.
This rhythmic process of inhaling and exhaling delivers oxygen to the alveoli and removes carbon dioxide, with its per-minute rate counted as a vital sign — what is it?
Breathing: Process of moving air in and out of the lungs.
With the formula CaC2, this industrial compound reacts with trace moisture to give off a garlicky smell and is used to generate acetylene gas in old-fashioned lamps — what is it?
Calcium carbide: Chemical compound. Its main use industrially is in the production of acetylene and calcium cyanamide.
This mammalian order of flesh-eating species is split into cat-like and dog-like suborders, Feliformia and Caniformia, and ranks as the sixth-largest order of mammals — which order?
Carnivora: Order of mammals. Carnivora ( kar-NIV-ər-ə) is an order of placental mammals specialised primarily in eating flesh, whose members are formally referred to as carnivorans.
Known in North America as fireweed and in Britain as rosebay willowherb, this perennial flowering plant thrives across the boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium: Species of flowering plant in the willowherb family.
This fluoroquinolone antibiotic treats everything from typhoid fever to urinary tract infections but can rarely cause tendon rupture — what drug?
Ciprofloxacin: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic. Ciprofloxacin, sold under the brand name Cipro among others, is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a number of bacterial infections.
This medical term describes inflammation of the large intestine, used both when the cause is undiagnosed and for its specific ulcerative form — what condition is it?
Colitis: Inflammation of the colon (large intestine). Colitis may be acute and self-limited or long-term.
This mostly inactive steroid hormone is created when an enzyme shields organs like the kidneys by converting active cortisol into its inactive form — what is it?
Cortisone: Corticosteroid precursor and metabolite of cortisol.
Started in 1955 by an army colonel and a cynologist as an experiment, this hybrid dog breed became officially recognized as a national breed in 1982 — which one?
Czechoslovakian Wolfdog: Czech and Slovak breed of dog.
Native to the Mediterranean and nicknamed 'clove pink' for a spicy fragrance reminiscent of cinnamon and nutmeg, what flower is this?
Dianthus caryophyllus: Species of flowering plant.
This Eastern Han hydrologist is credited as the first to harness a waterwheel to power the bellows of a blast furnace for forging cast iron — who was this ingenious engineer?
Du Shi: 1st-century engineer, metallurgist and politician.
The first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, this political scientist earned it in 2009 for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons — who was she?
This term covers a range of spiritual traditions built around hidden or occult knowledge, appearing in Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, and Quranic contexts alike — what is it?
Esotericism: Topics referred to by the same term.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'to lead out,' this scholarly practice of critically interpreting a text — often the Bible — also examines its historical background and literary genre — what is it called?
Exegesis: Critical investigation of a text.

Modern phylogenetics calls this a paraphyletic group covering nearly every vertebrate except the tetrapods — gill-bearing, limbless-of-digits, and usually cold-blooded. What aquatic animals are these?
Only chefs with three-plus years of rigorous training may legally prepare this potentially lethal Japanese pufferfish dish, whose poison is tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Ranging from Baja California to Japan's coast, this cephalopod is the largest of its kind on Earth and a common aquarium favorite — which creature?
Giant Pacific octopus: Species of cephalopod. It can be found from the intertidal zone down to 2,000 m (6,600 ft), and is best-adapted to colder, oxygen- and nutrient-rich waters.
One of China's 'Four Great Domestic Fish,' this herbivorous freshwater species was later introduced to Europe and the US to control aquatic weeds — which fish?
Grass carp: Species of fish. This Asian carp is the only species of the genus Ctenopharyngodon.
The son of a famous physicist and his first wife, this Swiss-American engineer taught hydraulic engineering at Berkeley and became renowned for research on sediment transport — who is he?

Hans Albert Einstein: Swiss-American engineer and educator. Hans Albert Einstein (May 14, 1904 – July 26, 1973) was a Swiss-American engineer, the second child and first son of physicists Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić.

First synthesized in 1940 by chemist Roger Adams via hydrogenation of THC isomers, this psychoactive cannabis-derived compound is sold in vaporizers despite never being drug-approved — which compound?
Lightest and most abundant element in the universe, it makes up about 75% of all normal matter and fuels the stars — colorless, odorless, and highly combustible. What element is it?
Hydrogen: Chemical element with atomic number 1 (H)
This contagious bacterial skin infection — usually from Staph or Strep — most often shows up as yellowish crusts on the face, arms or legs. What's it called?
Appointed FBI director by Barack Obama in 2013, this former federal prosecutor was fired from the post in 2017 — who is he?
Nicknamed "Marvellous Merchiston," this 16th-century Scottish laird discovered logarithms and popularized the decimal point — who was this mathematical wizard?

He coauthored the classic 1973 textbook Gravitation, advised Carl Sagan on wormholes for the novel Contact, and shared the 2017 Nobel Prize for the LIGO detection of gravitational waves — which astrophysicist?
Kip Thorne: American physicist, writer, and Nobel Laureate (born 1940)
This biennial vegetable in the onion family has an edible bundle of leaf sheaths sometimes colloquially called a 'stem' — what is it?
Leek: Vegetable in the onion family. A leek is a biennial vegetable, a cultivar of Allium ampeloprasum, the broadleaf wild leek (syn.
Tucked mostly beneath the right rib cage, this organ detoxifies the body, stores glucose as glycogen, and produces the bile that helps digest fat — which organ?
Liver: Vertebrate organ involved in metabolism.
First synthesized in 1912 by a Merck chemist, this stimulant known on the street as ecstasy or molly became linked to raves and electronic dance music in the 1980s — which drug?
MDMA: Psychoactive drug, often called ecstasy.
Whether a milk board's 'Got Milk?' campaign or a city pitching itself as a tourist destination, this discipline boils down to acquiring, satisfying, and retaining customers — what is it?
Marketing: Study and process of exploring, creating, and delivering value to customers.
More than 80% of cases of this cancer — which grows in the thin lining covering the lungs and other organs — trace back to asbestos exposure. What is it?
With over 17,000 built and flown by more than 50 countries, this Soviet-designed twin-turbine machine is the most-produced helicopter in the world — what is it?
Mil Mi-8: Family of transport helicopters.
Its wings make an odd whistling sound on take-off, and one pair may raise up to six broods a year — which abundant North American gamebird?
Mourning dove: North American bird in the family Columbidae.
Descended from Southern Italy's traditional guard dogs and closely related to the Cane Corso, this large wrinkly Italian breed was recognized in 1949 — which dog breed?
Neapolitan Mastiff: Italian breed of dog. The Neapolitan Mastiff or Mastino Napoletano is an Italian breed of large dog of mastiff type.

As the United States' first swept-wing fighter jet, this Korean War-era aircraft dueled Soviet MiG-15s in some of history's earliest jet-to-jet battles — which plane, produced in more than 7,800 units?
North American F-86 Sabre: Family of US fighter aircraft.

The world's most widespread and commercially important cactus species, this domesticated crop is grown both as a fruit and for its edible vegetable pads, likely originating in central Mexico — which species?
Opuntia ficus-indica: Species of cactus. It is grown primarily as a fruit crop, and also for the vegetable nopales and other uses.
One researcher catalogued as many as 549 varieties of this psychological category, defined by intense arousal toward things that aren't sexual by nature — what is the term?
In placental mammals, this is the region of the body between the anus and the genitals, running from the pubic bone to the tailbone, and is often considered an erogenous zone — what is it called?
Perineum: Region of the body between the genitals and anus. The perineum (pl.: perineums or perinea) in placental mammals is the space between the anus and the genitals.
Named after the Latin word for the magpie, a bird known for its opportunistic feeding habits, this eating disorder involves craving non-food objects — what is it?
Pica (disorder): Compulsive eating of non-food items.
Named from the Latin word for 'bridge' after Italian anatomist Costanzo Varolio, this brainstem structure sits above the medulla and below the midbrain — what is it?
Pons: Part of the brainstem in humans and other bipeds.
Named after a Russian explorer and reintroduced to Mongolia's steppes after going extinct in the wild, this rare equine has 33 chromosome pairs instead of the usual 32 — what species is it?
Colorless and odorless, this radioactive noble gas with atomic number 86 is a decay product of radium and eventually settles into stable isotopes of lead?
Radon: Chemical element with atomic number 86 (Rn)
Curving around the chest, these bones protect the lungs and heart and, in snakes, support and protect the whole body — what are they called?
Rib: Long bone in vertebrates that protects vital respiratory and cardiovascular organs.
First identified in Wuhan in late 2019 and once provisionally called 2019-nCoV, this positive-sense RNA virus is the one that causes COVID-19 — what's its official name?
SARS-CoV-2: Virus that causes COVID-19. The virus previously had the provisional name 2019 novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV), and has also been called human coronavirus 2019 (HCoV-19 or hCoV-19).
After early family-friendly Christian games found little success, which developer switched to horror in 2014 and created a hit franchise of horror video games?
Scott Cawthon: American video game developer (born 1978)
In this inherited blood disorder, faulty haemoglobin warps red cells into a rigid crescent shape that can't bend through capillaries, causing painful blockages — what is it?
Also known as milo, jowar, or Guinea corn, this grass — domesticated in Sudan and now grown worldwide — ranks as the fifth most important cereal crop on Earth — which grain?
Sorghum: Species of grain. It is typically an annual, but some cultivars are perennial.

In probability theory, this mathematical concept models a family of random variables indexed often by time, used to describe things like bacterial growth or a gas molecule's erratic path — what is it called?
Stochastic process: Collection of random variables. Stochastic processes are widely used as mathematical models of systems and phenomena that appear to vary in a random manner.
This medical term describes a resting heart rate that exceeds 100 beats per minute — what is it?
Tachycardia: Heart rate exceeding normal resting rate.
Often called the oldest form of drama, this collaborative art puts live performers before a live audience, blending gesture, speech, song, music and dance in one place — what is it?
